claims.wording: Chinese goods reached New Spain by way of Manila, in the Philippines, which the king of Spain also held. The crown set limits on the trade across the Pacific. Goods worth 250,000 pesos a year might come from the Philippines to New Spain in two ships, and 500,000 pesos in coin might go back. Only residents of the Philippines were to trade. Historians date these terms to 1593. In September 1603 the king restated them in a letter from Valladolid and wrote that they had been much exceeded.

claims.wording: On 6 May 1602 the city council of Mexico City told its agent at court to put one matter to the king before all others. claims.wording: In 1604 a poem in praise of Mexico City, Bernardo de Balbuena's *Grandeza Mexicana*, was printed in the city. It lists what the city gathered from the world: from the Philippines 'the cream', from Macao 'the most precious', from 'great China, coloured silks'. It says the city's wealth loads 'one fleet for Spain, another for China' each year, and that the city has by way of Manila 'all that the Chinese holds'. It is a poet praising his city to a patron, and shows what a resident boasted of, not what anyone counted. (Our translation.)

claims.wording: Historians explain the trade's pull on New Spain by price. Silver bought more in Asia than in Europe, and Chinese cloth cost much less in New Spain than what the fleets brought from Spain. Guillermina del Valle Pavón (2005) explains it this way. Woodrow Borah (1954) says the same of price, writing of merchants from Peru who bought in New Spain. José Luis Gasch-Tomás (2019) adds that Asian goods cost less in Spanish America than in Castile.

claims.wording: One man's account survives. In 1607 Gregorio Moreno petitioned the government at Seville. The record has him call himself 'an Indian of the Chinese nation from the Philippine islands'. It names an owner, don Lope de Ulloa. Moreno said he had been taken from his land and his parents' home, and carried to Mexico, to Peru, back to Mexico and then to Spain, 'more than 4,500 leagues', and was now 'helpless in a distant land'. The king granted him money for the journey home; the historian who found the case adds that it proved difficult for him to collect. His account reaches us through a petition, in a historian's English.
